title: Decisions
summary: Every decision so far: what we chose, why, and the catch. Replaced decisions stay listed and point to what replaced them.

items.title: Plan first, then build phase by phase with your sign-off
items.summary: Nine phases, P0 to P8. P0 is planning only, with no app code. A phase starts when you approve its plan and ends when its tests pass and you approve the result.
items.why: You asked to plan well before building, and to test rigorously, phase by phase.
items.catch: The first working app arrives later, and editing an approved page needs your re-approval.

items.title: The wiki is Claude's working memory
items.summary: Claude keeps plans, decisions and research as linked pages in the wiki (Karpathy's 'LLM wiki' pattern). Your raw notes are never edited; Claude maintains everything else.
items.why: You chose this pattern for documentation and decision making.
items.catch: Bookkeeping on every change, and the wiki can drift from the code; a before-commit warning (tested in P1) helps.

items.title: Work survives interrupted sessions
items.summary: After every task Claude updates the status page and the log. When a session ends it writes a handoff note, and the next session reads them and carries on.
items.why: You expect many sessions over many days, and sessions run out of tokens.
items.catch: Costs some time and tokens on every task.

items.title: A usable app and solid research, equally
items.summary: Each phase delivers something usable plus the measurement hooks the research needs. The app is never tuned just to win a benchmark.
items.why: You chose both goals with equal weight, built in lock-step.
items.catch: Convenience features with no research value (sidebar, split view) come late.

items.title: You install the developer tools (replaced)
items.summary: You would run the install commands Claude supplied; Claude would only check the versions afterwards.
items.why: Your first answer on how the tools get installed.
items.catch: Replaced: Claude now runs the installs and you click through the Windows prompts ([decision 21](ref:adr-0021)).

items.title: Browser controls in plain TypeScript, no UI framework
items.summary: Tab bar and address bar are plain TypeScript bundled by Vite. The controls never draw over the web page area.
items.why: Your choice: a small control panel with few dependencies.
items.catch: UI work is slower: shortcuts, tab dragging and accessibility are written by hand.

items.title: One window, many web views
items.summary: A trusted panel draws Ferrum's controls; each website tab is its own untrusted web view in the same window.
items.why: Your choice: it keeps websites apart from Ferrum's own trusted code.
items.catch: The Tauri feature for this is marked experimental and has open bugs (focus, resize, blank views).

items.title: Network log records what was fetched, never the content
items.summary: For each request Ferrum logs address, method, status, type, timing, size, tab and block decision, one line per request in a file. No headers, no page content.
items.why: Your choice: metadata only.
items.catch: Needs unsafe low-level WebView2 code, and full addresses can contain login tokens (whether to hide them is an open question to you).

items.title: Benchmarks run on your AMD desktop
items.summary: All measurements run on this machine. Energy is reported only as the CPU chip's own estimate, clearly labelled; whole-system energy only with a wall meter; per-program energy never.
items.why: Your choice of machine; research showed AMD's counters are estimates, so every claim must say so.
items.catch: Energy results are weaker than hoped without a wall meter, and reading the counters needs a driver you must approve.

items.title: Sites kept apart by profiles in one shared browser process
items.summary: Each site gets its own WebView2 profile (own cookies and storage) while all share one browser process. How to build it is still open and must be settled before P3.
items.why: Your choice: separate data per site without one browser process per site.
items.catch: Tauri cannot set a profile yet; you chose the low-level route in P1 (decision 29), which means more of our own code.

items.title: Git, GitHub checks, open licence; only you upload
items.summary: Code lives in git. Automatic checks run on GitHub's Windows machines. Licence: MIT or Apache 2.0. Claude never pushes; you create the GitHub repo and push.
items.why: Your choice: you stay in control of what gets published.
items.catch: The automatic checks cannot run until you create the GitHub repo.

items.title: Benchmark robot: Rust controller plus Playwright scripts
items.summary: A Rust program schedules trials and measures memory and CPU through Windows. Playwright scripts in TypeScript drive the pages. Every browser is driven the same way.
items.why: Your choice; one shared route for all browsers keeps the comparison fair.
items.catch: Every browser runs with a debugging connection attached, which may change results; a pilot measures its effect.

items.title: Statistics in Python scripts
items.summary: Analysis runs as repeatable Python scripts, not notebooks. Each comparison reports averages, spread, confidence ranges and effect sizes, with recorded random seeds.
items.why: Your choice when you picked the benchmark languages.
items.catch: A third language to keep pinned, and 30 trials per setup may be too few to see small differences.

items.title: You review the result of every phase
items.summary: At the end of every phase, planning included, Claude runs the tests, saves the output, writes a short report and stops. The next phase starts only after you approve the phase and then explicitly say go.
items.why: You asked to stop after each milestone for your review, on 10 Oct to pause after the planning phase and before building the next phase, and on 11 Oct confirmed the review applies to every phase.
items.catch: Progress waits on your review time.

items.title: Open browsing with a blocklist
items.summary: Any secure (HTTPS) site opens unless blocked. Plain HTTP is upgraded or warned about. Other link types (mail, apps) ask first. Local files and address-bar scripts are refused in tabs.
items.why: Your choice: normal browsing, with guard rails where they matter.
items.catch: A blocklist is advice, not a sandbox, so security tests must be thorough; Google sign-in will likely fail in tabs.

items.title: Plan app reads the wiki and takes approvals (replaced)
items.summary: A local Next.js app would show the wiki pages, and you would click Approve there.
items.why: Your first request for an interactive plan.
items.catch: Replaced: you approve in Claude Code, and the portal is read-only ([decision 23](ref:adr-0023)).

items.title: Research paper in the ACM LaTeX template, for now
items.summary: The paper uses ACM's acmart template until a venue is chosen. Text stays portable, and no results section is written until experiments are done.
items.why: One template covers many ACM formats; the venue is not chosen yet.
items.catch: If the venue is IEEE or USENIX, the paper has to be moved to another template.

items.title: Repo folder is the project folder; Rust code in one workspace
items.summary: The planned folder layout (app, libraries, benchmarks, analysis, paper) sits directly at the repo root, plus folders for the baseline app, the benchmark robot and the throwaway test builds (kept as evidence). You approved it on 11 Oct.
items.why: Shorter Windows paths, and the wiki and plan sit beside the code.
items.catch: Slightly differs from the original drawing; that the Tauri tool builds the app inside this layout is checked in P2.

items.title: Unsafe WebView2 code lives in one audited module
items.summary: Features Tauri lacks (sleep, memory target, network events, crash detection) use raw WebView2 calls, all in one module behind a safe Rust interface. Two small Windows modules for measuring memory and CPU may also use unsafe code, each with its own safety notes. You approved it on 11 Oct.
items.why: Unsafe code must be documented and contained, and Tauri does not offer these features.
items.catch: More design work in P2; whether it coexists with Tauri's own handlers is not checked yet.

items.title: Wiki index lists evidence folders, not every file
items.summary: The wiki index names each evidence folder once instead of every file in it.
items.why: Your choice; it scales to the many files benchmark runs will create.
items.catch: The index no longer names each evidence file; phase pages and the log still do.

items.title: Claude runs all tool installs
items.summary: Claude runs the install commands, including ones that need admin rights (you click through the Windows prompts), and records exact versions. Kernel drivers still need your separate approval.
items.why: Your choice: it saves you the manual steps.
items.catch: Claude's installs change the machine; the saved version records are the audit trail.

items.title: A broken approvals file stops the wiki check
items.summary: If the approvals file is unreadable or approves a missing page, the wiki check now fails instead of only warning. A decision you rejected is also flagged.
items.why: Two rules contradicted each other, and a corrupt approvals file passed the check.
items.catch: Claude decided this under your delegation; you can overturn it.

items.title: You approve in Claude Code; the portal is read-only
items.summary: You say what you approve in Claude Code. Claude saves your words, then records the approval with a fingerprint of the page. If the page changes later, Claude asks again.
items.why: You want to steer through Claude Code only; the portal is just for tracking.
items.catch: Claude now writes the approvals file, so only one tested script may do it, and every change is logged.

items.title: The portal shows only plain-language JSON
items.summary: Whenever Claude edits the wiki, it rewrites the matching plain-language JSON in the same step. The portal reads only that JSON, never the wiki; it also shows, read-only, the check scripts that JSON names.
items.why: You want plain words, not a wiki rendered in a web page.
items.catch: Every wiki edit needs a second write; a check script and a hook catch misses.

items.title: Check scripts in PowerShell 7
items.summary: Every task gets one script that proves it is done, and every phase one gate script that runs all its checks. Each part is commented in plain words.
items.why: You asked for scripts you can read and re-run.
items.catch: More files to maintain; a script can drift from its task, but the gate script runs them all.

items.title: Architecture in four groups
items.summary: Components are shown as Application, Benchmark, Testing and quality, and Research and analysis, led by a layered picture of the Rust app.
items.why: You found the component graph incomprehensible and asked for a clear split.
items.catch: The grouping lives in this decision and the portal, not on each component page.

items.title: Mask private network and machine details
items.summary: Real IP addresses, machine names, network card ids and your user-folder path are replaced by placeholders. Real values stay in one local file that git ignores.
items.why: You asked that such details never sit in the repo.
items.catch: Masked evidence is no longer byte-for-byte original, and old values stay in local history until a rewrite you approve.

items.title: Browser look: tabs on top, Ferrum panel on the right
items.summary: The browser has tabs across the top, an address bar with a lock and a shield button, the website in the middle, and a Ferrum panel on the right with memory, CPU, sleeping tabs, blocked sites and this tab's network log. No AI assistant.
items.why: Your choice (option A of three): everything Ferrum knows about your tabs is visible at a glance.
items.catch: The panel takes about 352 pixels. Its sections stay empty until later stages build blocking, memory measuring, the network log and tab sleep. Tabs in the top bar need a custom title bar: [open question](ref:Q-125). Values are samples.

items.title: Ferrum creates the tab views itself, one profile per site
items.summary: Each tab is a web view Ferrum creates with the engine's own call, using Tauri's environment and a profile name per site; the shell stays a normal Tauri view. You approved it on 11 Oct.
items.why: It is the only tested way that gives each site its own profile inside one shared browser, as you chose.
items.catch: More low-level code to maintain, and Tauri's ready-made tab hooks must be rebuilt with engine events in phase 2. That tab pages get no path to the app's commands is expected but not yet tested (P2).

items.title: Back and forward ask the browser, not the page
items.summary: The back and forward buttons use the engine's own history calls and its "history changed" signal. You approved it on 11 Oct.
items.why: The browser knows whether back is possible, so the buttons are always right, and no script is put into web pages.
items.catch: One more low-level event per tab; cross-site navigation in per-site mode may still lose history (open question).

items.title: One test robot path for every browser, visible tab only
items.summary: Benchmarks drive Ferrum, Chrome and Edge with the same Playwright code over the debugging channel, measure only the tab on screen, and group each product's processes with a Windows job. You approved it on 11 Oct.
items.why: The same driving code and flags for everyone keeps the comparison fair.
items.catch: The debugging channel exposes all views on the computer, so it is only for benchmark runs; its own overhead is checked in P6.

items.title: Bookmarks and history in a local file, moved by encrypted backup
items.summary: Bookmarks and history live in one SQLite database file on your PC. To move them to another Ferrum, you export one backup file locked with a passphrase you choose, and import it there: you see what's inside first, then merge or replace. Cookies and logins are never included.
items.why: You chose SQLite over Postgres: nothing to install or run, works offline, fast search, and no extra process to skew the benchmarks. The backup is your 'manual, but secure' dump.
items.catch: No automatic sync between PCs. A lost passphrase means the backup cannot be opened. Built with standard, published building blocks (SQLite; Argon2id and XChaCha20-Poly1305 from RustCrypto), all passing the licence check.

items.title: New look: Graphite, split-tile logo, themes ready
items.summary: Your pick: look A in Graphite colours, dark and metallic, light or dark following Windows; logo 8, the split tile, for now. Themes are built as swappable colour sets, so more themes can be added later without rewriting the browser.
items.why: You chose it on the design canvas, and asked that themes can be configured in the future.
items.catch: It replaces the calm warm-grey colours of 10 Oct (the layout stays). Only Graphite ships now; a theme picker comes when a second theme exists.
